name: John Adams
role: Second president of the United States (1797-1801), Revolutionary leader and author of the Massachusetts Constitution of 1780
summary: John Adams was a Revolutionary leader and Federalist who defended republican government built on a mixed constitution: separated powers, a strong independent executive, a second chamber and independent judges, as checks on any single majority or elite. He held that property must be secure, that suffrage should rest on property, that natural inequalities are unavoidable, and that religion and morals underpin free government. He opposed hereditary monarchy for America, held to neutrality in foreign affairs, abhorred slavery while favouring gradual abolition, and signed and later defended the Alien and Sedition Acts.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Inferred: he listed taxes laid heavy on the rich, and not on others, among the abuses a propertyless majority would vote itself; he gave no view on a particular tax rate.

property-fundamental.rationale: Wrote that property is a right of mankind as real as liberty and that once property is no longer held as sacred as the laws of God, anarchy and tyranny begin; his draft Declaration of Rights bars taking property without consent of the people or their representatives.

state-harmful.rationale: Wrote that a legislator who said the law of nature is enough and no government is necessary would be thought to trifle; government was for him the means of social happiness.

limit-guns.rationale: His draft Declaration of Rights states a right to keep and bear arms for the common defence, and in Thoughts on Government he wanted a militia law requiring men to be provided with arms.

decide-locally.rationale: In 1776 he wanted a continental authority confined to war, trade and a few other matters, but he later supported a strong federal constitution.

more-religion-public.rationale: His draft let the legislature require towns to support public worship and enjoin attendance, he proclaimed national fasts, and he wrote that the Constitution was made only for a moral and religious people.

gradual-change.rationale: Urged Massachusetts to be very cautious about altering the established qualifications of voters and said abolishing slavery must be gradual; but he also led a revolution, so the evidence is partly mixed.

revolution-justified.rationale: Led the case for American independence and in 1818 described the Revolution as a radical change in the principles and sentiments of the people that preceded the war; wrote that he was borne by an irresistible sense of duty.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Told James Sullivan in 1776 that the balance of power follows the balance of landed property, so land should be easy to acquire and divided into small parcels so that the multitude holds it.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Praised the English limited monarchy as the most stupendous fabric of human invention, yet called himself a mortal and irreconcilable enemy to monarchy and no friend to hereditary limited monarchy in America; Wikipedia describes his views as shifting.

democracy-best.rationale: Called a republic the best government but wrote that simple democracy never lasts and commits suicide, preferring a mixed constitution with checks on popular majorities; the evidence is mixed.

direct-votes.rationale: Wrote that in a large society the people cannot assemble to make laws, so power must be deputed to a few of the wise and good; later wrote that democracy soon wastes, exhausts and murders itself.

natural-rulers.rationale: Held that natural aristocracy (superiority of influence arising from human nature) is unavoidable and wanted the wise and good deputed to the legislature and senate, while keeping it checked.

separate-church-state.rationale: His draft Declaration of Rights authorized public support of worship and teachers of religion and morals at public expense and required the governor to profess the Christian religion.

equal-outcomes.rationale: In his letters to John Taylor he rejected equalizing property: an equal division today would be undone within a month, and he asked whether Taylor professed himself a downright leveller.

conscription.rationale: His draft Declaration of Rights says each citizen must give personal service, or an equivalent, when necessary for the protection the society provides.

universal-morality.rationale: Called the general principles of Christianity eternal and immutable and treated the law of nature and the decalogue as binding standards behind civil law.

single-common-good.rationale: Held that the competing interests of rich and poor, few and many cannot be dissolved and must be balanced by separate branches or one will oppress the other.

national-self-determination.rationale: Argued in Novanglus and in Congress that the colonies had the right to govern themselves under their own legislatures, ending in independence.

night-watchman-state.rationale: His Thoughts on Government and Massachusetts draft assigned the state education, support of public worship, sumptuary laws and promotion of virtue beyond defence and justice.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: His draft Declaration of Rights begins that all men are born equally free and independent, and he held slavery in abhorrence; he also accepted natural inequalities and a property franchise.

consent-of-governed.rationale: His draft Declaration of Rights states that the people alone have an incontestable, unalienable right to institute, reform or change government, and that no tax or law binds them without their or their representatives' consent.

separated-powers.rationale: Argued in Thoughts on Government and the Defence that legislative, executive and judicial power must be separate and check one another, and that the legislature itself needs more than one branch.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Signed and later defended the Alien and Sedition laws as war measures he believed constitutional and salutary, but his draft Declaration also bars suspension of laws except by the legislature.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Listed regulation of prices with paper money and tender laws as horrors that stared him in the face during the quasi-war.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Proposed that the governor command the militia and armies and, with council advice and consent, appoint judges and officers; his Massachusetts draft made the governor commander-in-chief.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Wrote in 1778 that he wanted no political connection or military assistance from France, only commerce, and in 1797 that Americans have seen enough of perpetual alliances.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Treated property as a right prior to and as sacred as law, protected against takings without consent, not justified only by its service to the common good.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Asked in his 1797 inaugural whether robes and diamonds add anything essential to government, and wrote that if sovereignty were a divine right there would be an end of the rights of mankind.

character-from-environment.rationale: Said education contributes to the formation of mind and heart as nature does, while also holding that virtues and vices often run in families.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Defined good government as an empire of laws, and his draft Declaration says the power of suspending laws belongs only to the legislature, never to a single man.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Held that only a mixed government of the one, the few and the many, in three independent branches, controls faction; he called the English balanced constitution the most stupendous fabric of human invention.

land-redistribution.rationale: Wrote against majority schemes of agrarian laws and a general division of property, which he said would end in anarchy and tyranny.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Argued that in a single sovereign assembly the majority is omnipotent and the minority defenceless, and urged independent judges, a separate executive and a second chamber as barriers against majority power.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: His draft Declaration of Rights calls the idea of a man born a magistrate, lawgiver or judge absurd and unnatural, and he denied wanting hereditary monarchy or aristocracy for America; he did praise the English hereditary orders for England.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Drafted the Declaration of Rights placed ahead of the Massachusetts frame of government as a statement of rights the legislature could not override (jury trial, search warrants, press, no taking of property without consent).

elective-rulers.rationale: In his 1797 inaugural he praised government in which the executive and legislators are selected at regular periods by their neighbours over authority descending from antiquity; his Massachusetts draft made governor and legislators elective.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: In Novanglus he argued that resistance is justified once repeated oppression shows rulers have formed a settled plan to deprive the people of their liberties; his draft Declaration affirms the right to reform or change government.

military-guardian-role.rationale: His draft Declaration of Rights says the military power shall always be held in exact subordination to the civil authority, and that standing armies in peace are dangerous to liberty.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: His draft required all money to leave the treasury by warrant agreeably to the acts and resolves of the legislature, and the Defence endorses the commons withholding supplies.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Argued that frugality cures vanities, levities and fopperies and favoured sumptuary laws; his draft Declaration calls for piety, temperance, industry and frugality.

religion-illusion.rationale: Wrote that the general principles of Christianity are as eternal and immutable as the existence and attributes of God and called Christianity the religion of reason, equity and love.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Wrote in the Declaration of Rights draft that all power resides originally in the people and is derived from them, and denounced the divine theory under which resistance to any government is blasphemy.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: As president he held to neutrality among the European belligerents, wrote that he was determined not to be entangled in the wars of Europe, and refused a perpetual alliance with Britain.

dynastic-succession.rationale: His draft Declaration of Rights calls the idea of a man born a magistrate, lawgiver or judge absurd and unnatural, and in 1797 he asked whether authority descending from accidents could be more respectable than that springing from the people.

property-franchise.rationale: Told James Sullivan in 1776 not to change voter qualifications and defended fixing a property qualification; his Massachusetts draft required freehold income of three pounds or an estate of sixty pounds to vote.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Defined a republic as an empire of laws and not of men and wrote into his draft Declaration that rights are protected according to standing laws and that only the legislature may suspend laws.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Feared an oligarchy of the wealthy and held that the power of the rich had to be channelled by separate institutions; wrote that an aristocracy of land-jobbers and stock-jobbers was entailed on the country.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Inferred: he held religion and virtue to be the only foundations of republican government and wanted public worship supported, which excludes state promotion of atheism.

second-chamber.rationale: Insisted a single assembly would grow avaricious, ambitious and arbitrary, and proposed a separate council or senate with a negative voice in legislation; his Massachusetts draft created a Senate.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Agreed with Rush that religion and virtue are the only foundations of republicanism and of social felicity, and wrote a duty to worship the Supreme Being into his draft constitution.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Wrote that the passions are the same in all men under all forms of government and rejected the perfectibility of the human mind as a doctrine, allowing only gradual amelioration.

women-suffrage.rationale: In 1776 he argued against widening the franchise, warning that women would demand a vote, and treated women as dependent like propertyless men; wrote jokingly to Abigail against repealing masculine systems.

national-church-status.rationale: Wrote in 1811 that he would as soon establish the Episcopal or Catholic church as a national Presbyterian establishment, and rejected a national establishment; his Massachusetts draft supported public worship generally, not one church.

simple-living.rationale: Praised frugality, simplicity and sobriety as standards of morality and a revenue-saving virtue, but never urged self-sufficiency.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Wrote that the funding system was contrived to enrich particular individuals at public expense and that every bank of discount was corruption that taxes the public for the benefit of individuals.

notes: Historical figure: answers come from his own writings and drafts, not inference, except where a rationale begins "Inferred:". Wikipedia says he signed the Alien and Sedition Acts at the urging of his wife and cabinet without having promoted them; he later wrote that he believed the alien and sedition laws constitutional and salutary. His views on monarchy and hereditary institutions are described as shifting. His draft of the Massachusetts constitution was altered by the convention on points such as the religion article.
